title: Γλαῦκος καὶ Διομήδης
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Hector leaves for the city, his great shield knocking at his ankles and neck, and between the two armies Diomedes meets a man he does not know. He asks who he is, saying that he will not fight a god, and tells how Lycurgus, who chased Dionysus’ nurses from Nyseion, was blinded by Zeus and soon died. The stranger asks why Diomedes wants his lineage, since men are like leaves: the wind scatters some, the forest puts forth others, and the generations of men grow and pass. Then he gives it all the same. He is Glaucus, descended from Sisyphus of Ephyre, and his grandfather was Bellerophon, whom King Proetus sent to Lycia with a tablet of marks that was to have him killed, after Proetus’ wife Anteia lied about him. The Lycian king set him against the Chimaera, the Solymi and the Amazons, then against an ambush, and when he survived all of it gave him his daughter and half his honour. Glaucus’ father was Bellerophon’s son Hippolochus, and Zeus fathered Sarpedon on Bellerophon’s daughter. Diomedes is glad, plants his spear in the ground and says that his grandfather Oeneus once entertained Bellerophon, so that the two men are guest-friends from their fathers’ time. They will keep out of each other’s way in the fighting and exchange armour.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἀπέβη κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.tr: hōs ara phōnēsas apebē korythaiolos Hektōr·
sentences.l: So then, having spoken, went away Hector of the glancing helmet;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Hector of the glancing helmet went off;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἀπέβη ‘so then, having spoken, he went away’ is a formula for leaving after a speech. Hector has said (113) that he will go to Ilios to have the elders and the wives pray and promise sacrifices, and this is his going; the Greek here says only ἀπέβη, aorist of ἀποβαίνω ‘go away’. κορυθαίολος ‘of the glancing helmet’ (κόρυς ‘helmet’ and αἰόλος ‘quick-moving, glancing’) is his stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δέ μιν σφυρὰ τύπτε καὶ αὐχένα δέρμα κελαινὸν
ἄντυξ ἣ πυμάτη θέεν ἀσπίδος ὀμφαλοέσσης.
sentences.tr:
amphi de min sphyra typte kai auchena derma kelainon
antyx hē pymatē theen aspidos omphaloessēs.
sentences.l:
And about him struck at ankles and neck the dark hide,
the rim which ran outermost of the bossed shield.
sentences.i: Round him the dark hide, the outermost rim of his bossed shield, struck against his ankles and his neck.
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ δέ μιν … τύπτε is ‘and about him … struck’, with the subject held back to the end of the line: δέρμα κελαινὸν ‘the dark hide’, which the next line names as ἄντυξ ‘rim’. Here ἄντυξ is the rim of a shield (elsewhere it is a chariot’s rail), πυμάτη ‘last’ means outermost, and ὀμφαλοέσσης ‘bossed’ is from ὀμφαλός, the ‘navel’ or boss at the centre. σφυρά ‘ankles’ and αὐχένα ‘neck’ are the two things struck. The picture is of a shield large enough to reach from neck to ankle, as the ‘man-covering shield’ of 2.389 does, swinging against him as he walks. τύπτε and θέεν (for θέε, with movable ν) are unaugmented imperfects.

sentences.t:
Γλαῦκος δ’ Ἱππολόχοιο πάϊς καὶ Τυδέος υἱὸς
ἐς μέσον ἀμφοτέρων συνίτην μεμαῶτε μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
Glaukos d’ Hippolochoio païs kai Tydeos huios
es meson amphoterōn synitēn memaōte machesthai.
sentences.l:
And Glaucus, Hippolochus’ son, and the son of Tydeus
into the midst of both came together, the two eager to fight.
sentences.i: Glaucus, son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus came together into the space between the two armies, both of them eager to fight.
sentences.n: Two subjects, Γλαῦκος and Τυδέος υἱός, take a dual verb, συνίτην ‘the two came together’ (imperfect of σύνειμι, from εἶμι ‘go’), and a dual participle, μεμαῶτε ‘both eager’ (perfect of μέμονα). The son of Tydeus is Diomedes, who is named at 122; Glaucus is introduced only by his father, and where he comes from becomes clear in his story (Lycia, 171 ff.). ἐς μέσον ἀμφοτέρων ‘into the middle of both’ leaves the word ‘armies’ unsaid, and the English supplies it.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ σχεδὸν ἦσαν ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ἰόντε,
τὸν πρότερος προσέειπε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hote dē schedon ēsan ep’ allēloisin ionte,
ton proteros proseeipe boēn agathos Diomēdēs·
sentences.l:
And when now near they were, upon one another advancing,
him first addressed, good at the war-cry, Diomedes:
sentences.i: When they had come near, advancing on one another, Diomedes, good at the war-cry, was the first to speak to him:
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ is the article used as a pronoun, and ἰόντε is a dual participle ‘going’, the pair advancing together. In τὸν πρότερος προσέειπε, τόν is Glaucus (‘him’) and πρότερος ‘first’ agrees with Διομήδης: Diomedes is the first to speak. βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is his stock epithet. προσέειπε is the epic spelling of προσεῖπε ‘addressed’. The colon opens his speech.

sentences.t: τίς δὲ σύ ἐσσι φέριστε καταθνητῶν ἀνθρώπων;
sentences.tr: tis de sy essi pheriste katathnētōn anthrōpōn;
sentences.l: “And who are you, best of mortal men?
sentences.i: “Who are you, then, best of mortal men?
sentences.n: Diomedes asks the name he has not got. φέριστε is the vocative of φέριστος ‘best’, with the genitive καταθνητῶν ἀνθρώπων ‘of mortal men’; the genitive could instead hang on τίς (‘who of mortal men?’), and the sense is the same. σύ ἐσσι is ‘you are’ (ἐσσί is the epic 2nd singular of εἰμί). δέ ‘and’ in a question links it to what he has just seen. The question mark is the Greek ;.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ ποτ’ ὄπωπα μάχῃ ἔνι κυδιανείρῃ
τὸ πρίν·
sentences.tr:
ou men gar pot’ opōpa machēi eni kydianeirēi
to prin·
sentences.l:
For never yet have I seen you in the man-glorifying battle
before;
sentences.i: For I have never before seen you in the battle that brings men glory;
sentences.n: ὄπωπα is the perfect of ὁράω, ‘have seen’, and its object is left out (the English supplies ‘you’). μάχῃ ἔνι is ἐν μάχῃ, with the preposition after its noun and so accented. κυδιανείρῃ ‘man-glorifying’ is κῦδος ‘glory’ with ἀνήρ ‘man’, the stock adjective of battle. τὸ πρίν is ‘before this’. The sentence stops in the middle of the line, at the ano teleia, and a new one begins.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ μὲν νῦν γε πολὺ προβέβηκας ἁπάντων
σῷ θάρσει, ὅ τ’ ἐμὸν δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος ἔμεινας·
sentences.tr:
atar men nyn ge poly probebēkas hapantōn
sōi tharsei, ho t’ emon dolichoskion enchos emeinas·
sentences.l:
but indeed now at least far you have stepped forward beyond all
in your courage, in that my long-shadowed spear you have awaited;
sentences.i: but now you have gone far beyond all others in your courage, in that you have awaited my long-shadowed spear;
sentences.n: ἀτὰρ μὲν νῦν γε ‘but yet now, at least’ sets the present against ‘never before’. προβέβηκας is the perfect of προβαίνω ‘step forward’, with πολὺ … ἁπάντων ‘far beyond all’ (genitive of comparison), and σῷ θάρσει ‘by your courage’ is a dative of cause. ὅ τ’ is ὅ τε, here a conjunction ‘in that, because’. ἔμεινας is μένω ‘wait for, stand to face’ with an accusative, the spear. δολιχόσκιον ‘long-shadowed’ is the stock epithet of ἔγχος ‘spear’, translated every time.

sentences.t: δυστήνων δέ τε παῖδες ἐμῷ μένει ἀντιόωσιν.
sentences.tr: dystēnōn de te paides emōi menei antioōsin.
sentences.l: And of wretched men the sons my might meet.
sentences.i: It is the sons of wretched men who meet my might.
sentences.n: A boast in the form of a general truth (δέ τε, with the epic τε of what is always so): only the unlucky face him. δυστήνων ‘of wretched men’ is the genitive of δύστηνος, the word that is ‘wretched’ everywhere. ἀντιόωσιν is the uncontracted, stretched form of ἀντιῶσι, from ἀντιάω ‘meet’, and it takes the dative ἐμῷ μένει ‘my might’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ τις ἀθανάτων γε κατ’ οὐρανοῦ εἰλήλουθας,
οὐκ ἂν ἔγωγε θεοῖσιν ἐπουρανίοισι μαχοίμην.
sentences.tr:
ei de tis athanatōn ge kat’ ouranou eilēlouthas,
ouk an egōge theoisin epouranioisi machoimēn.
sentences.l:
But if some one of the immortals, down from heaven you have come,
not would I, for my part, with the gods of heaven fight.
sentences.i: But if you are one of the immortals and have come down from heaven, I at least would not fight against the gods of heaven.
sentences.n: τις … εἰλήλουθας is ‘you, some one of the immortals, have come’: the indefinite τις stands in the nominative with a second-person verb. εἰλήλουθας is the perfect of ἔρχομαι, and κατ’ οὐρανοῦ is ‘down from heaven’ (κατά with the genitive). ἐπουρανίοισι (ἐπί with οὐρανός) ‘of heaven’ is the adjective of the gods who live there. οὐκ ἂν … μαχοίμην is the optative with ἂν, ‘would not fight’, and μάχομαι takes the dative of the opponent; ἔγωγε is ‘I for my part’. In Book 5 he did in fact wound two gods, Aphrodite (5.335 ff.) and Ares (5.855 ff.), with Athena’s leave and help.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδὲ Δρύαντος υἱὸς κρατερὸς Λυκόοργος
δὴν ἦν, ὅς ῥα θεοῖσιν ἐπουρανίοισιν ἔριζεν·
sentences.tr:
oude gar oude Dryantos huios krateros Lykoorgos
dēn ēn, hos rha theoisin epouranioisin erizen·
sentences.l:
For not even the son of Dryas, strong Lycurgus,
long was he, who with the gods of heaven quarrelled;
sentences.i: For not even the son of Dryas, strong Lycurgus, lived long, he who quarrelled with the gods of heaven;
sentences.n: οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδέ is ‘for not even’. Δρύαντος υἱός is ‘son of Dryas’, and Λυκόοργος is the uncontracted form of the name that appears as Λυκούργου in 134. κρατερός ‘strong’ is a stock epithet, translated every time. δὴν ἦν, literally ‘was long’, means ‘lived long’, and it comes again at 139–140. ὅς ῥα ‘who, as is known’ introduces the offence; ἔριζεν is ἐρίζω ‘quarrel, contend’, here an open war on gods, with the dative. Diomedes tells the story as a warning.

sentences.t:
ὅς ποτε μαινομένοιο Διωνύσοιο τιθήνας
σεῦε κατ’ ἠγάθεον Νυσήϊον·
sentences.tr:
hos pote mainomenoio Diōnysoio tithēnas
seue kat’ ēgatheon Nysēïon·
sentences.l:
who once of raging Dionysus the nurses
drove down the holy Nyseion;
sentences.i: who once chased the nurses of raging Dionysus down the holy Nyseion;
sentences.n: Διωνύσοιο is the epic genitive of Διώνυσος, and μαινομένοιο ‘raging’ is the participle of μαίνομαι, the god’s frenzy. τιθήνας is ‘nurses’ (τιθήνη), the women who brought him up. σεῦε is an unaugmented past tense of σεύω ‘drive, chase’, and κατά with the accusative is ‘down along’. Νυσήϊον is an adjective used as a noun, ‘the Nysian (place)’; its place is not known. ἠγάθεος ‘holy’ is the house word. The · stops the sentence in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
αἳ δ’ ἅμα πᾶσαι
θύσθλα χαμαὶ κατέχευαν ὑπ’ ἀνδροφόνοιο Λυκούργου
θεινόμεναι βουπλῆγι·
sentences.tr:
hai d’ hama pasai
thysthla chamai katecheuan hyp’ androphonoio Lykourgou
theinomenai bouplēgi·
sentences.i: and they all let their sacred implements fall to the ground, as they were struck by man-slaying Lycurgus with an ox-goad;
sentences.n: αἳ δ’ is ‘and they’, the nurses, with ἅμα πᾶσαι ‘all together’. θύσθλα occurs only here; it is traditionally taken as the sacred implements of the god’s rites, but the exact meaning is not known. κατέχευαν is the aorist of καταχέω ‘pour down’; of things it comes to mean ‘let fall’. θεινόμεναι ‘being struck’ is a passive participle, ὑπ’ … Λυκούργου ‘by Lycurgus’ names the agent, and βουπλήξ is the ox-goad (βοῦς ‘ox’ with πλήσσω ‘strike’) in the dative of means. ἀνδροφόνος ‘man-slaying’ is the stock epithet, kept even though it is only too fitting here.

sentences.t:
Διώνυσος δὲ φοβηθεὶς
δύσεθ’ ἁλὸς κατὰ κῦμα, Θέτις δ’ ὑπεδέξατο κόλπῳ
δειδιότα·
sentences.tr:
Diōnysos de phobētheis
dyseth’ halos kata kyma, Thetis d’ hypedexato kolpōi
deidiota·
sentences.i: and Dionysus, in fear, went down into the wave of the sea, and Thetis received him in her bosom, terrified as he was;
sentences.n: φοβηθείς is an aorist passive participle ‘frightened’, and δύσεθ’ is ἐδύσετο, the unaugmented aorist middle of δύω ‘go down into’ (the verb, with ἀνα- ‘up’, that brought Thetis up out of the wave at 1.496), with κατά and the accusative ‘down into the wave’. Thetis is the sea-goddess; ὑπεδέξατο is ‘received’, and κόλπῳ is ‘in her bosom’ (κόλπος also means ‘gulf, bay’). δειδιότα is the accusative of a perfect participle of δείδω ‘fear’, agreeing with the unnamed god, ‘terrified’.

sentences.t: κρατερὸς γὰρ ἔχε τρόμος ἀνδρὸς ὁμοκλῇ.
sentences.tr: krateros gar eche tromos andros homoklēi.
sentences.l: for strong trembling held him at the man’s rebuke.
sentences.i: for strong trembling held him at the man’s shouted rebuke.
sentences.n: κρατερός ‘strong’ goes with τρόμος ‘trembling’, and ἔχε ‘held’ has as its object the god, who is not named again. ἀνδρός ‘of the man’ is Lycurgus, and ὁμοκλῇ is a dative of cause. ὁμοκλή is a shouting at someone, a threat or an order, and the house word for it is ‘rebuke’. γάρ gives the reason for the god’s flight.

sentences.t:
τῷ μὲν ἔπειτ’ ὀδύσαντο θεοὶ ῥεῖα ζώοντες,
καί μιν τυφλὸν ἔθηκε Κρόνου πάϊς·
sentences.tr:
tōi men epeit’ odysanto theoi rheia zōontes,
kai min typhlon ethēke Kronou païs·
sentences.l:
With him then were angry the gods who live at ease,
and blind him made the son of Cronus;
sentences.i: Then the gods who live at ease were angry with him, and the son of Cronus made him blind;
sentences.n: τῷ μέν is ‘with him’, the dative of the one they were angry with (Lycurgus; the μέν has no matching δέ). ὀδύσαντο is the aorist middle of ὀδύσσομαι ‘be angry with’. θεοὶ ῥεῖα ζώοντες ‘the gods who live at ease’ is a stock phrase: the gods’ life has no trouble in it. μιν is ‘him’, τυφλόν ‘blind’, and Κρόνου πάϊς ‘the son of Cronus’ is Zeus, whom Diomedes does not name.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτι δὴν
ἦν, ἐπεὶ ἀθανάτοισιν ἀπήχθετο πᾶσι θεοῖσιν·
sentences.tr:
oud’ ar’ eti dēn
ēn, epei athanatoisin apēchtheto pasi theoisin·
sentences.l:
nor then any longer for long
was he, since to the immortals he was hateful, all the gods;
sentences.i: and he did not live long after that, since he was hateful to all the immortal gods;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτι δὴν ἦν is ‘nor then any longer was he for long’, that is, he did not live much longer; δὴν ἦν is the phrase of 131. ἀπήχθετο is the aorist of ἀπεχθάνομαι ‘become hateful to’, with the dative, and it takes the house word ‘was hateful’; it returns at 200, of Bellerophon. ἀθανάτοισιν … πᾶσι θεοῖσιν ‘to the immortals, all the gods’ is emphatic: he was hateful to every god, not to Zeus alone.

sentences.t: οὐδ’ ἂν ἐγὼ μακάρεσσι θεοῖς ἐθέλοιμι μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr: oud’ an egō makaressi theois etheloimi machesthai.
sentences.l: Nor would I wish with the blessed gods to fight.
sentences.i: Nor would I wish to fight against the blessed gods.
sentences.n: Diomedes draws his conclusion. μάκαρες θεοί ‘the blessed gods’ is a stock phrase, and ἐθέλοιμι is the optative of ἐθέλω ‘wish’, with the infinitive μάχεσθαι, which takes the dative of the opponent, as in 129.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ τίς ἐσσι βροτῶν οἳ ἀρούρης καρπὸν ἔδουσιν,
ἆσσον ἴθ’ ὥς κεν θᾶσσον ὀλέθρου πείραθ’ ἵκηαι.
sentences.tr:
ei de tis essi brotōn hoi arourēs karpon edousin,
asson ith’ hōs ken thasson olethrou peirath’ hikēai.
sentences.l:
But if you are one of mortals who the fruit of the plough-land eat,
nearer come, so that sooner the limits of destruction you may reach.”
sentences.i: But if you are one of the mortals who eat the fruit of the plough-land, come nearer, so that you may reach the limits of destruction the sooner.”
sentences.n: εἰ δέ τίς ἐσσι βροτῶν is ‘but if you are one of mortals’, the second of his two cases (the first was a god, 128). ἀρούρης καρπὸν ἔδουσιν ‘eat the fruit of the plough-land’ describes ordinary mortals by their food; ἔδουσιν is the epic form of ἐσθίουσι. ἆσσον ἴθ’ ‘come nearer’ is a challenge (ἆσσον is the comparative of ἄγχι ‘near’, ἴθι the imperative of εἶμι). ὥς κεν … ἵκηαι is ‘so that you may reach’ (ὥς ‘so that’, κεν = ἄν, ἵκηαι an epic aorist subjunctive), and θᾶσσον is ‘more quickly’. ὀλέθρου πείραθα ‘the limits of destruction’ is the point at which destruction is reached. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖθ’ Ἱππολόχοιο προσηύδα φαίδιμος υἱός·
sentences.tr: ton d’ auth’ Hippolochoio prosēuda phaidimos huios·
sentences.l: And him in turn Hippolochus’ glorious son addressed:
sentences.i: Then Hippolochus’ glorious son spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The paragraph break marks the change of speaker. αὖθ’ is αὖτε ‘in turn’, and προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘address’. φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ is the stock epithet of υἱός, and the son of Hippolochus is Glaucus.

sentences.t: Τυδεΐδη μεγάθυμε τί ἢ γενεὴν ἐρεείνεις;
sentences.tr: Tydeïdē megathyme ti ē geneēn ereeineis;
sentences.l: “Tydeus’-son, great-hearted, why indeed do you ask my lineage?
sentences.i: “Great-hearted son of Tydeus, why do you ask about my lineage?
sentences.n: Glaucus takes ‘who are you?’ as a question about his family. Τυδεΐδη is the vocative of the patronymic ‘son of Tydeus’, and μεγάθυμε ‘great-hearted’ is a stock epithet. τί ἢ … ‘why indeed …’: the particle after τί sharpens the question. ἐρεείνεις is the epic ‘ask about’. γενεή covers ‘descent, lineage’ here, and in the next lines ‘generation’; the English has to use two words for one.

sentences.t: οἵη περ φύλλων γενεὴ τοίη δὲ καὶ ἀνδρῶν.
sentences.tr: hoiē per phyllōn geneē toiē de kai andrōn.
sentences.l: Such as is the generation of leaves, such also is that of men.
sentences.i: As is the generation of leaves, so too is that of men.
sentences.n: οἵη περ … τοίη δὲ καί is ‘just such as … such also’, two correlative feminines agreeing with γενεή, which now means a generation, all those born at about the same time. This is his whole answer to the question of lineage: the lines that follow only unfold it. φύλλων and ἀνδρῶν are genitives of the thing whose generation it is.

sentences.t:
φύλλα τὰ μέν τ’ ἄνεμος χαμάδις χέει, ἄλλα δέ θ’ ὕλη
τηλεθόωσα φύει, ἔαρος δ’ ἐπιγίγνεται ὥρη·
sentences.tr:
phylla ta men t’ anemos chamadis cheei, alla de th’ hylē
tēlethoōsa phyei, earos d’ epigignetai hōrē·
sentences.l:
Leaves, some the wind to the ground pours, and others the forest,
thriving, puts forth, and of spring comes on the season;
sentences.i: The wind scatters some of the leaves on the ground, while the thriving forest puts forth others, and the season of spring comes on;
sentences.n: φύλλα τὰ μέν … ἄλλα δέ is ‘leaves, some … and others’: τὰ μέν is the object of χέει and ἄλλα that of φύει; τ’ and θ’ are the epic τε of what happens every year. χαμάδις ‘to the ground’ is an adverb, and χέει is ‘pours’. ὕλη is the forest, and τηλεθόωσα (from τηλεθάω) ‘thriving’ is used of growing things. φύει is transitive here, ‘puts forth’. ἔαρος … ὥρη is ‘the season of spring’, and ἐπιγίγνεται ‘comes on’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἀνδρῶν γενεὴ ἣ μὲν φύει ἣ δ’ ἀπολήγει.
sentences.tr: hōs andrōn geneē hē men phyei hē d’ apolēgei.
sentences.l: So of men the generation: one grows, and one ceases.
sentences.i: So it is with the generation of men: one springs up and another ceases.
sentences.n: ἣ μὲν … ἣ δέ is ‘the one … the other’, one generation and another. φύει, which put forth leaves in 148, is now intransitive, ‘grows, springs up’, and ἀπολήγει is ‘ceases, comes to an end’. The point is that a generation does not last and is replaced.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἐθέλεις καὶ ταῦτα δαήμεναι ὄφρ’ ἐῢ εἰδῇς
ἡμετέρην γενεήν, πολλοὶ δέ μιν ἄνδρες ἴσασιν·
sentences.tr:
ei d’ etheleis kai tauta daēmenai ophr’ eÿ eidēis
hēmeterēn geneēn, polloi de min andres isasin·
sentences.l:
But if you wish also these things to learn, so that well you may know
our lineage — and many men know it —
sentences.i: But if you also wish to learn this, so that you may know our lineage well (and many men know it):
sentences.n: εἰ δ’ ἐθέλεις is ‘but if you wish’, ταῦτα ‘these things’ is what follows, δαήμεναι is the epic aorist infinitive of δάω ‘learn’ (= δαῆναι), and ὄφρ’ ἐῢ εἰδῇς is ‘so that you may know well’ (subjunctive of οἶδα). ἡμετέρην ‘our’ is the family’s, and μιν ‘it’ is the lineage; ἴσασιν is ‘they know’. The sentence never gets its main clause (‘then listen’): the story itself takes its place.

sentences.t:
ἔστι πόλις Ἐφύρη μυχῷ Ἄργεος ἱπποβότοιο,
ἔνθα δὲ Σίσυφος ἔσκεν, ὃ κέρδιστος γένετ’ ἀνδρῶν,
Σίσυφος Αἰολίδης·
sentences.tr:
esti polis Ephyrē mychōi Argeos hippobotoio,
entha de Sisyphos esken, ho kerdistos genet’ andrōn,
Sisyphos Aiolidēs·
sentences.i: There is a city, Ephyre, in a corner of horse-pasturing Argos, and there lived Sisyphus, who proved the shrewdest of men — Sisyphus, son of Aeolus;
sentences.n: Ἐφύρη is the city, usually identified with the later Corinth; μυχῷ is ‘in the innermost part, in a recess’, and ἱππόβοτος ‘horse-pasturing’ is the stock epithet of Argos, the land in a corner of which the city lies. ἔσκεν is an old form of ‘was’ in -σκ-, ‘lived’, and γένετ’ is ἐγένετο ‘became, proved’. κέρδιστος is the superlative of the κέρδος ‘gain, advantage’ family (compare κέρδιον ‘better’): the one who best knew how to turn things to his advantage. Αἰολίδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Aeolus’. The sentence ends with the name repeated.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄρα Γλαῦκον τέκεθ’ υἱόν,
αὐτὰρ Γλαῦκος τίκτεν ἀμύμονα Βελλεροφόντην·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ara Glaukon teketh’ huion,
autar Glaukos tikten amymona Bellerophontēn·
sentences.l:
and he begot Glaucus as a son,
and Glaucus begot blameless Bellerophon;
sentences.i: and he begot a son, Glaucus, and Glaucus begot blameless Bellerophon;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ἄρα ‘and he’ is Sisyphus. τέκεθ’ is ἐτέκετο, the aorist middle of τίκτω, used of a father, ‘begot’; τίκτεν is an unaugmented imperfect. This first Glaucus is the great-grandfather of the speaker (the Bellerophon of this line fathers Hippolochus, 197). ἀμύμων ‘blameless’ is a stock epithet, and the real sense of the word is not known.

sentences.t:
τῷ δὲ θεοὶ κάλλός τε καὶ ἠνορέην ἐρατεινὴν
ὤπασαν·
sentences.tr:
tōi de theoi kallos te kai ēnoreēn erateinēn
ōpasan·
sentences.l:
To him the gods beauty and manliness, lovely,
granted;
sentences.i: The gods granted him beauty and lovely manliness;
sentences.n: τῷ ‘to him’ is Bellerophon (the article as a pronoun). κάλλος is ‘beauty’ and ἠνορέη ‘manliness’ (from ἀνήρ), the qualities of a young man, with ἐρατεινήν ‘lovely’ agreeing with the second. ὤπασαν is the aorist of ὀπάζω ‘grant, give besides’.

sentences.t:
αὐτάρ οἱ Προῖτος κακὰ μήσατο θυμῷ,
ὅς ῥ’ ἐκ δήμου ἔλασσεν, ἐπεὶ πολὺ φέρτερος ἦεν,
Ἀργείων·
sentences.tr:
autar hoi Proitos kaka mēsato thymōi,
hos rh’ ek dēmou elassen, epei poly pherteros ēen,
Argeiōn·
sentences.i: but Proetus devised evil against him in his heart, and drove him out of the land, since he was far stronger than the Argives;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ οἱ is ‘but against him’ (οἱ is a dative of disadvantage), and κακὰ μήσατο is the aorist middle of μήδομαι ‘devise’. ὅς ῥ’ is ὅς ῥα ‘who, as follows’; ἐκ δήμου ἔλασσεν is ‘drove (him) out of the land’, with the object left out. φέρτερος is the comparative ‘stronger’, followed by the genitive Ἀργείων ‘than the Argives’, which stands at the head of the next line. The next unit says why the king was so strong. Bellerophon’s offence is not in the Greek here.

sentences.t: Ζεὺς γάρ οἱ ὑπὸ σκήπτρῳ ἐδάμασσε.
sentences.tr: Zeus gar hoi hypo skēptrōi edamasse.
sentences.l: for Zeus to him under the sceptre subdued (them).
sentences.i: for Zeus had made them subject to his sceptre.
sentences.n: Ζεὺς γάρ gives the cause of Proetus’ strength. οἱ ‘to him’ is Proetus, ὑπὸ σκήπτρῳ is ‘under the sceptre’ (the sceptre is the sign of a king), and ἐδάμασσε is the aorist of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, with its object, the Argives, left out; the English supplies ‘them’ and uses a pluperfect because the clause explains what was already so.

sentences.t:
τῷ δὲ γυνὴ Προίτου ἐπεμήνατο δῖ’ Ἄντεια
κρυπταδίῃ φιλότητι μιγήμεναι·
sentences.tr:
tōi de gynē Proitou epemēnato di’ Anteia
kryptadiēi philotēti migēmenai·
sentences.l:
And for him the wife of Proetus went mad, heavenly Anteia,
in secret love to be mingled;
sentences.i: And the wife of Proetus, heavenly Anteia, went mad with desire for him, to lie with him in secret love;
sentences.n: τῷ δέ ‘and for him’ is Bellerophon, and ἐπεμήνατο is the aorist of ἐπιμαίνομαι ‘go mad for’. The infinitive μιγήμεναι ‘to be mingled’ (aorist passive of μίγνυμι) says what she wanted: ‘mingled in love’ is the poem’s way of saying lie with. κρυπταδίῃ ‘secret’ comes from κρύπτω ‘hide’. δῖα ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet and stays on her, though she is about to lie.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τὸν οὔ τι
πεῖθ’ ἀγαθὰ φρονέοντα δαΐφρονα Βελλεροφόντην.
sentences.tr:
alla ton ou ti
peith’ agatha phroneonta daïphrona Bellerophontēn.
sentences.l:
but him not at all
was she persuading, thinking good thoughts, wise-minded Bellerophon.
sentences.i: but she did not at all persuade him, wise-hearted Bellerophon, who thought good thoughts.
sentences.n: πεῖθ’ is ἔπειθε, the imperfect of πείθω, ‘was trying to persuade’; the English past ‘did not persuade’ gives the outcome. τόν ‘him’ stands first and the name comes at the end. ἀγαθὰ φρονέοντα is ‘thinking good thoughts, of good mind’, and δαΐφρονα is the stock epithet ‘wise-minded’ (l) and ‘wise-hearted’ (i); whether it means ‘wise’ or ‘fierce’ is disputed.

sentences.t: ἣ δὲ ψευσαμένη Προῖτον βασιλῆα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: hē de pseusamenē Proiton basilēa prosēuda·
sentences.l: And she, having lied, addressed king Proetus:
sentences.i: And lying, she spoke to king Proetus:
sentences.n: ἣ δὲ ‘and she’ is Anteia. ψευσαμένη is the aorist participle of ψεύδομαι ‘speak falsely, lie’: the poet tells us what her words are before we hear them. βασιλῆα is the epic accusative of βασιλεύς ‘king’. Her words, which Glaucus reports inside his own speech, take single quotation marks.

sentences.t:
τεθναίης ὦ Προῖτ’, ἢ κάκτανε Βελλεροφόντην,
ὅς μ’ ἔθελεν φιλότητι μιγήμεναι οὐκ ἐθελούσῃ.
sentences.tr:
tethnaiēs ō Proit’, ē kaktane Bellerophontēn,
hos m’ ethelen philotēti migēmenai ouk ethelousēi.
sentences.l:
‘May you be dead, Proetus, or kill Bellerophon,
who wished to be mingled with me in love, me not wishing.’
sentences.i: ‘May you die, Proetus, or else kill Bellerophon, who wished to lie with me in love when I did not wish it.’
sentences.n: Anteia turns the truth round: it was she who wished it (160–162). τεθναίης is the perfect optative of θνῄσκω, ‘may you be dead’ (a wish aimed at him), and ὦ Προῖτ’ is a vocative. κάκτανε is the aorist imperative of κατακτείνω ‘kill’ (κατ- changed to κακ- before κτ-). ὅς μ’ ἔθελεν is ‘who wished (to)’, with the infinitive μιγήμεναι ‘to be mingled’, and οὐκ ἐθελούσῃ is a dative agreeing with an unstated μοι, ‘with me, not wishing’.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τὸν δὲ ἄνακτα χόλος λάβεν οἷον ἄκουσε·
sentences.tr: hōs phato, ton de anakta cholos laben hoion akouse·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and the lord anger seized, at such a thing as he heard;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and anger seized the lord at what he heard;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο ‘so she spoke’ closes her words. τὸν δὲ ἄνακτα is ‘and him, the lord’, Proetus (ἄναξ ‘lord’ for the man called βασιλεύς ‘king’ in 163). χόλος λάβεν is ‘anger seized (him)’, λάβεν being ἔλαβε without the augment. οἷον ἄκουσε is ‘such a thing as he heard’, a cry of what it was he heard; ἄκουσε is unaugmented. Anger (χόλος) is anger, not the wrath (μῆνις) of the poem’s first word.

sentences.t:
κτεῖναι μέν ῥ’ ἀλέεινε, σεβάσσατο γὰρ τό γε θυμῷ,
πέμπε δέ μιν Λυκίην δέ, πόρεν δ’ ὅ γε σήματα λυγρὰ
γράψας ἐν πίνακι πτυκτῷ θυμοφθόρα πολλά,
δεῖξαι δ’ ἠνώγειν ᾧ πενθερῷ ὄφρ’ ἀπόλοιτο.
sentences.tr:
kteinai men rh’ aleeine, sebassato gar to ge thymōi,
pempe de min Lykiēn de, poren d’ ho ge sēmata lygra
grapsas en pinaki ptyktōi thymophthora polla,
deixai d’ ēnōgein hōi pentherōi ophr’ apoloito.
sentences.l:
to kill him indeed he avoided, for he felt awe at this in his heart,
but he sent him to Lycia, and gave him grievous signs,
having scratched in a folded tablet many heart-destroying ones,
and had bidden him show them to his own father-in-law, that he might perish.
sentences.i: He shunned killing him, for he felt awe at that in his heart; but he sent him to Lycia and gave him grievous signs, having inscribed many heart-destroying ones on a folded tablet, and ordered him to show them to his own father-in-law, so that Bellerophon might die.
sentences.n: κτεῖναι μέν ῥ’ ἀλέεινε is ‘to kill indeed he avoided’ (ἀλεείνω ‘avoid, shun’; the object of κτεῖναι, ‘him’, is left out). σεβάσσατο is the aorist of σεβάζομαι ‘feel awe’; why he felt it is not said. Λυκίην δέ is Λυκίηνδε ‘to Lycia’, the suffix -δε printed as a separate word. γράψας is from γράφω ‘scratch’ (as in ἐπέγραψε ‘grazed’, 4.139) and also ‘write’; the signs were only marks on a πίναξ πτυκτός ‘folded tablet’. θυμοφθόρα ‘heart-destroying’ is a rare word of unclear sense. ἠνώγειν is a pluperfect of ἄνωγα used as a past ‘ordered’; ᾧ is ‘his own’, not ‘whom’; the πενθερός, a wife’s father, is Anteia’s, the Lycian king. The subject of ὄφρ’ ἀπόλοιτο is Bellerophon, whom the English names. The four lines make one sentence.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὁ βῆ Λυκίην δὲ θεῶν ὑπ’ ἀμύμονι πομπῇ.
sentences.tr: autar ho bē Lykiēn de theōn hyp’ amymoni pompēi.
sentences.l: But he went to Lycia under the blameless escort of the gods.
sentences.i: He went to Lycia under the blameless escort of the gods.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὁ ‘but he’ is Bellerophon, βῆ is ἔβη without its augment, and Λυκίην δέ is ‘to Lycia’ again. θεῶν ὑπ’ ἀμύμονι πομπῇ is ‘under the blameless escort of the gods’, with ὑπ’ placed between genitive and noun. πομπή is ‘escort’, and ἀμύμων ‘blameless’ is the stock epithet, here of the escort. The gods protect him on a mission meant to destroy him.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ Λυκίην ἷξε Ξάνθόν τε ῥέοντα,
προφρονέως μιν τῖεν ἄναξ Λυκίης εὐρείης·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē Lykiēn hixe Xanthon te rheonta,
prophroneōs min tien anax Lykiēs eureiēs·
sentences.l:
But when he came to Lycia and the flowing Xanthus,
readily him honoured the lord of wide Lycia;
sentences.i: But when he reached Lycia and the flowing Xanthus, the lord of wide Lycia honoured him readily;
sentences.n: ἷξε is the aorist of ἵκω ‘come to’, with two accusatives, Λυκίην and Ξάνθον. This Xanthus is the river of Lycia; the Trojan river of 6.4 has the same name. προφρονέως is ‘readily, with a ready mind’, and τῖεν is the unaugmented imperfect of τίω ‘honour’. ἄναξ Λυκίης εὐρείης is ‘lord of wide Lycia’; the king is not named here.

sentences.t: ἐννῆμαρ ξείνισσε καὶ ἐννέα βοῦς ἱέρευσεν.
sentences.tr: ennēmar xeinisse kai ennea bous hiereusen.
sentences.l: For nine days he entertained him as a guest, and nine oxen he slaughtered.
sentences.i: For nine days he entertained him as his guest, and slaughtered nine oxen.
sentences.n: ἐννῆμαρ is ‘for nine days’, an adverb. ξείνισσε is ‘entertained as a guest’ (from ξεῖνος), and ἱέρευσεν ‘slaughtered’, nine oxen for nine days suggests one a day, but the Greek does not say so. Hospitality comes first, and the questions come on the tenth day.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ δεκάτη ἐφάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠὼς
καὶ τότε μιν ἐρέεινε καὶ ᾔτεε σῆμα ἰδέσθαι
ὅττί ῥά οἱ γαμβροῖο πάρα Προίτοιο φέροιτο.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē dekatē ephanē rhododaktylos Ēōs
kai tote min ereeine kai ēitee sēma idesthai
hotti rha hoi gambroio para Proitoio pheroito.
sentences.l:
But when the tenth appeared, rose-fingered Dawn,
then he questioned him and asked to see the sign,
whatever from his son-in-law Proetus he was bringing him.
sentences.i: But when the tenth rose-fingered Dawn appeared, then he questioned him and asked to see the sign, whatever he was bringing him from his son-in-law Proetus.
sentences.n: δεκάτη ‘tenth’ agrees with Ἠώς ‘Dawn’, so ‘the tenth Dawn appeared’, and ῥοδοδάκτυλος ‘rose-fingered’ is her stock epithet. ἐρέεινε is ‘questioned’, and ᾔτεε the uncontracted imperfect of αἰτέω ‘ask for’. σῆμα ἰδέσθαι is ‘to see the sign’. ὅττι … φέροιτο is ‘whatever he was bringing’, an indirect question in the optative after a past tense, with οἱ ‘to him’ and γαμβροῖο … Προίτοιο ‘from his son-in-law Proetus’; πάρα is παρά ‘from’, placed after its noun. γαμβρός is the husband of one’s daughter.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ σῆμα κακὸν παρεδέξατο γαμβροῦ,
πρῶτον μέν ῥα Χίμαιραν ἀμαιμακέτην ἐκέλευσε
πεφνέμεν·
sentences.tr:
autar epei dē sēma kakon paredexato gambrou,
prōton men rha Chimairan amaimaketēn ekeleuse
pephnemen·
sentences.i: And when the king had received the evil sign from his son-in-law, he first ordered him to kill the Chimaera, that huge creature;
sentences.n: παρεδέξατο is the aorist middle of παραδέχομαι ‘receive’, with the genitive γαμβροῦ ‘from his son-in-law’, and κακὸν σῆμα is ‘the evil sign’, the tablet’s message. πρῶτον μέν ῥα ‘first indeed’ opens a list of labours, continued by δεύτερον (184) and τὸ τρίτον (186). Χίμαιραν is the monster’s name, and the next unit shows she is also, in her middle, a χίμαιρα ‘she-goat’. ἀμαιμακέτην is a word whose meaning is not known (the Odyssey uses it of a mast, ‘huge’; ‘irresistible’ is the other guess). ἐκέλευσε ‘ordered’ takes the infinitive πεφνέμεν, the epic infinitive of the old aorist ἔπεφνον ‘killed’. The subject, the Lycian king, is not named; the English names him.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔην θεῖον γένος οὐδ’ ἀνθρώπων,
πρόσθε λέων, ὄπιθεν δὲ δράκων, μέσση δὲ χίμαιρα,
δεινὸν ἀποπνείουσα πυρὸς μένος αἰθομένοιο,
καὶ τὴν μὲν κατέπεφνε θεῶν τεράεσσι πιθήσας.
sentences.tr:
hē d’ ar’ eēn theion genos oud’ anthrōpōn,
prosthe leōn, opithen de drakōn, messē de chimaira,
deinon apopneiousa pyros menos aithomenoio,
kai tēn men katepephne theōn teraessi pithēsas.
sentences.l:
and she was of divine stock, not of men,
in front a lion, behind a serpent, and in the middle a she-goat,
dreadfully breathing out the might of blazing fire,
and her indeed he killed, of the gods the portents having obeyed.
sentences.i: She was of divine stock, not of men: a lion in front, a serpent behind, and a she-goat in the middle, dreadfully breathing out the might of blazing fire; and he killed her, obeying the portents of the gods.
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔην is ‘and she was’ (ἔην is the epic ἦν). θεῖον γένος is ‘of divine stock’, an accusative of respect. The three parts are given in order; the last, with a small χ, is the ordinary word for a she-goat, χίμαιρα. δεινόν is an adverb ‘dreadfully’, ἀποπνείουσα ‘breathing out’, and μένος πυρός ‘the might of fire’ is a periphrasis for fire itself, like βίη Ἡρακληείη (2.658); αἰθομένοιο ‘blazing’. κατέπεφνε ‘killed’ has an intensifying κατα-. πιθήσας is the aorist participle of πείθομαι ‘obey’, and θεῶν τεράεσσι πιθήσας is the clause of 4.398, where Tydeus lets Maeon go: both heroes act on signs from the gods.

sentences.t: δεύτερον αὖ Σολύμοισι μαχέσσατο κυδαλίμοισι·
sentences.tr: deuteron au Solymoisi machessato kydalimoisi·
sentences.l: Second, in turn, the glorious Solymi he fought;
sentences.i: Next he fought the glorious Solymi;
sentences.n: δεύτερον αὖ is ‘second, in turn’. μαχέσσατο is the aorist of μάχομαι, which takes the dative of the enemy, Σολύμοισι, so the English says ‘fought the Solymi’. The Solymi are a people whose country is not given here; they return at 204. κυδαλίμοισι ‘glorious’ is the stock epithet.

sentences.t: καρτίστην δὴ τήν γε μάχην φάτο δύμεναι ἀνδρῶν.
sentences.tr: kartistēn dē tēn ge machēn phato dymenai andrōn.
sentences.l: The strongest, indeed, that fighting at least, he said he had entered, of men.
sentences.i: That, he said, was the strongest fighting of men that he had entered.
sentences.n: καρτίστην ‘strongest’ is the superlative of καρτερός, qualifying μάχην ‘fighting’; the house word for μάχη is ‘fighting’, as at 3.241 ‘enter the fighting of men’. τήν γε is ‘that one at least’. φάτο ‘he said’ is Bellerophon, whose own words about the Solymi Glaucus gives. δύμεναι is the epic aorist infinitive of δύω ‘enter’, as if the fight were a place one goes into. ἀνδρῶν ‘of men’ goes with μάχην: ‘the fighting of men’.

sentences.t: τὸ τρίτον αὖ κατέπεφνεν Ἀμαζόνας ἀντιανείρας.
sentences.tr: to triton au katepephnen Amazonas antianeiras.
sentences.l: Third, in turn, he killed the Amazons, man-matching.
sentences.i: Third, he killed the man-matching Amazons.
sentences.n: τὸ τρίτον αὖ is ‘third, in turn’, completing the series. ἀντιανείρας is ‘man-matching’ (ἀντί with ἀνήρ); whether it means ‘a match for men’, ‘fighting like men’ or ‘opposed to men’ is disputed. Ἀμαζόνες is the Greek name, kept in its English form.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἄρ’ ἀνερχομένῳ πυκινὸν δόλον ἄλλον ὕφαινε·
sentences.tr: tōi d’ ar’ anerchomenōi pykinon dolon allon hyphaine·
sentences.l: And for him as he came back a solid trick, another, he wove;
sentences.i: And as he was coming back, the king wove another trick against him, a closely woven one;
sentences.n: τῷ … ἀνερχομένῳ is ‘for him as he was coming back’ (ἀνέρχομαι ‘go up, return up’), a dative of the one aimed at. πυκινὸν δόλον is ‘a solid trick’: πυκινός is ‘dense, close-packed’ (the house word is ‘solid’, as in the Cadmeans’ πυκινὸν λόχον, 4.392), and with ὕφαινε ‘wove’ it suggests a closely woven web. ἄλλον ‘another’ counts the tablet as the first trick. The subject is still the Lycian king, whom the English names.

sentences.t:
κρίνας ἐκ Λυκίης εὐρείης φῶτας ἀρίστους
εἷσε λόχον·
sentences.tr:
krinas ek Lykiēs eureiēs phōtas aristous
heise lochon·
sentences.l:
having chosen out of wide Lycia the best men
he set an ambush;
sentences.i: He picked out the best men from wide Lycia and set an ambush;
sentences.n: κρίνας is the aorist participle of κρίνω; the Iliad’s usual ‘sort’ would not fit a selection of the best men, so it is ‘choose, pick out’ here. φῶτας ἀρίστους is ‘the best men’ (φώς ‘man’), and εὐρείης ‘wide’ is repeated from 173. εἷσε is the aorist of ἵζω in its transitive use, ‘made sit, set’, and λόχος ‘ambush’ is both the men in hiding and the plan.

sentences.t: τοὶ δ’ οὔ τι πάλιν οἶκον δὲ νέοντο·
sentences.tr: toi d’ ou ti palin oikon de neonto·
sentences.l: and they not at all back homeward returned;
sentences.i: and they did not come back home at all;
sentences.n: τοὶ δ’ is ‘and they’ (the article used as a pronoun, with the accent the edition prints). οὔ τι is ‘not at all’, and οἶκον δέ is οἶκόνδε ‘homeward’, again printed as two words. νέοντο is a form of νέομαι ‘go, come back’. The reason follows.

sentences.t: πάντας γὰρ κατέπεφνεν ἀμύμων Βελλεροφόντης.
sentences.tr: pantas gar katepephnen amymōn Bellerophontēs.
sentences.l: for all he killed, blameless Bellerophon.
sentences.i: for blameless Bellerophon killed them all.
sentences.n: πάντας ‘all’ is thrown to the front. κατέπεφνεν is ‘killed’. The stock epithet ἀμύμων ‘blameless’ stays on Bellerophon as he kills a whole band of men, and the sense of the word is not known. This is his fourth exploit in the king’s service, after the Chimaera, the Solymi and the Amazons.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ γίγνωσκε θεοῦ γόνον ἠῢν ἐόντα
αὐτοῦ μιν κατέρυκε, δίδου δ’ ὅ γε θυγατέρα ἥν,
δῶκε δέ οἱ τιμῆς βασιληΐδος ἥμισυ πάσης·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē gignōske theou gonon ēÿn eonta
autou min kateryke, didou d’ ho ge thygatera hēn,
dōke de hoi timēs basilēïdos hēmisy pasēs·
sentences.i: But when the king came to see that Bellerophon was the good offspring of a god, he kept him there, and gave him his own daughter, and gave him half of all his royal honour;
sentences.n: γίγνωσκε is the imperfect, ‘was coming to know’. The participle ἐόντα ‘being’ goes with an unstated ‘him’: ‘recognised him as being’. θεοῦ γόνον ἠῢν is ‘a good offspring of a god’ (ἠΰς is the epic ἐΰς ‘good’), and the Greek does not say which god. αὐτοῦ is ‘there, on the spot’, and κατέρυκε ‘held back, kept’. δίδου is an imperfect of giving, English ‘gave’, and ἥν is ‘his own’ (the possessive, not the relative). τιμῆς βασιληΐδος ἥμισυ πάσης is ‘half of all the royal honour’, τιμή being a king’s standing and privileges. Line 192 is metrically irregular as transmitted: θυγατέρα has its first syllable lengthened in the fifth foot, and its short last syllable stands in the long place of the sixth, before ἥν.

sentences.t:
καὶ μέν οἱ Λύκιοι τέμενος τάμον ἔξοχον ἄλλων
καλὸν φυταλιῆς καὶ ἀρούρης, ὄφρα νέμοιτο.
sentences.tr:
kai men hoi Lykioi temenos tamon exochon allōn
kalon phytaliēs kai arourēs, ophra nemoito.
sentences.l:
And indeed for him the Lycians a precinct cut out, standing out above others,
fine, of planted land and of plough-land, that he might occupy it.
sentences.i: And the Lycians for their part set apart for him an estate that stood out above others, a fine one of planted land and plough-land, for him to occupy.
sentences.n: καὶ μέν οἱ is ‘and indeed for him’. τέμενος is a plot cut off for a king or a god, from the same root as τάμον, the aorist of τάμνω ‘cut’: ‘cut out’. The house words are ‘precinct’ (l) and ‘estate’ (i). ἔξοχον ἄλλων is ‘standing out above others’. φυταλιῆς ‘planted land’ is a rare word for ground set with trees or vines, and with ἀρούρης ‘plough-land’ it is a genitive of respect, ‘fine for …’. ὄφρα νέμοιτο is ‘that he might occupy’ (optative of purpose; νέμομαι ‘hold and use’).

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἔτεκε τρία τέκνα δαΐφρονι Βελλεροφόντῃ
Ἴσανδρόν τε καὶ Ἱππόλοχον καὶ Λαοδάμειαν.
sentences.tr:
hē d’ eteke tria tekna daïphroni Bellerophontēi
Isandron te kai Hippolochon kai Laodameian.
sentences.l:
And she bore three children to wise-minded Bellerophon,
Isander and Hippolochus and Laodamia.
sentences.i: She bore wise-hearted Bellerophon three children: Isander, Hippolochus and Laodamia.
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ ‘and she’ is the Lycian king’s daughter. ἔτεκε is ‘bore’, the mother’s verb (a father ‘begets’, 155). The three names stand in apposition to τρία τέκνα. δαΐφρονι is ‘wise-minded’ (l) and ‘wise-hearted’ (i). Ἱππόλοχον is the speaker’s own father: Glaucus has reached his own place in the story. Laodamia is a woman, Bellerophon’s daughter.

sentences.t:
Λαοδαμείῃ μὲν παρελέξατο μητίετα Ζεύς,
ἣ δ’ ἔτεκ’ ἀντίθεον Σαρπηδόνα χαλκοκορυστήν.
sentences.tr:
Laodameiēi men parelexato mētieta Zeus,
hē d’ etek’ antitheon Sarpēdona chalkokorystēn.
sentences.l:
With Laodamia lay counsellor Zeus,
and she bore godlike Sarpedon, bronze-armed.
sentences.i: Zeus the counsellor lay with Laodamia, and she bore godlike Sarpedon, armed in bronze.
sentences.n: παρελέξατο is ‘lay beside’ (aorist of παραλέγομαι), and in English ‘lay with’. μητίετα Ζεύς is ‘Zeus the counsellor’ (μητίετα, from μῆτις ‘counsel’, is translated even when the counsellor’s business is this). Σαρπηδών is therefore the speaker’s cousin. ἀντίθεος ‘godlike’ and χαλκοκορυστής (l ‘bronze-armed’, i ‘armed in bronze’; the second part is from κορύσσω ‘arm’) are stock epithets.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ καὶ κεῖνος ἀπήχθετο πᾶσι θεοῖσιν,
ἤτοι ὃ κὰπ πεδίον τὸ Ἀλήϊον οἶος ἀλᾶτο
ὃν θυμὸν κατέδων, πάτον ἀνθρώπων ἀλεείνων·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē kai keinos apēchtheto pasi theoisin,
ētoi ho kap pedion to Alēïon oios alato
hon thymon katedōn, paton anthrōpōn aleeinōn·
sentences.i: But when he too was hateful to all the gods, then he wandered alone over the Aleian plain, eating his own heart, shunning the paths of men;
sentences.n: κεῖνος is ἐκεῖνος ‘that man too’: Bellerophon, like Lycurgus. ἀπήχθετο πᾶσι θεοῖσιν is the clause of 140, and the Greek gives no reason for his fall. ἤτοι ὃ is ‘then he, for his part’ (the edition prints ἤτοι as one word). κὰπ is κατά, and Ἀλήϊον ‘the Aleian (plain)’ sounds like ἀλᾶτο ‘wandered’, the next word but one. The poet seems to play on the likeness. οἶος is ‘alone’; ἀλᾶτο is the unaugmented imperfect of ἀλάομαι ‘wander’. ὃν θυμὸν κατέδων ‘eating his own heart’ is an image of grief. πάτον is ‘path’, and ἀλεείνων is the verb of 167, ‘avoiding’.

sentences.t:
Ἴσανδρον δέ οἱ υἱὸν Ἄρης ἆτος πολέμοιο
μαρνάμενον Σολύμοισι κατέκτανε κυδαλίμοισι·
sentences.tr:
Isandron de hoi huion Arēs atos polemoio
marnamenon Solymoisi katektane kydalimoisi·
sentences.l:
And Isander, his son, Ares, insatiate of war,
fighting the Solymi killed, the glorious ones;
sentences.i: And Isander, his son, Ares, who never has enough of war, killed as he fought the glorious Solymi;
sentences.n: Ἴσανδρον … υἱὸν is ‘Isander, his son’ (οἱ is ‘his’, Bellerophon’s), put first as the object. Ἄρης ἆτος πολέμοιο is ‘Ares, insatiate of war’; Ares is the god himself here. μαρνάμενον is the present participle of μάρναμαι ‘fight’ with the dative Σολύμοισι, ‘fighting the Solymi’, the people his father had fought (184).

sentences.t: τὴν δὲ χολωσαμένη χρυσήνιος Ἄρτεμις ἔκτα.
sentences.tr: tēn de cholōsamenē chrysēnios Artemis ekta.
sentences.l: And her, angered, golden-reined Artemis killed.
sentences.i: And in anger golden-reined Artemis killed her.
sentences.n: τὴν is ‘her’, Laodamia. χολωσαμένη is the aorist participle of χολόομαι ‘be angered’ (from χόλος ‘anger’); the Greek does not say why. χρυσήνιος ‘golden-reined’ (χρυσός with ἡνία ‘rein’) is the stock epithet the Odyssey gives to Ares and here goes to Artemis. ἔκτα is the aorist of κτείνω ‘killed’. Of Bellerophon’s three children two die here, Isander and Laodamia; the third, Hippolochus, lives to be Glaucus’ father.

sentences.t: Ἱππόλοχος δέ μ’ ἔτικτε, καὶ ἐκ τοῦ φημι γενέσθαι·
sentences.tr: Hippolochos de m’ etikte, kai ek tou phēmi genesthai·
sentences.l: And Hippolochus begot me, and from him I say that I was born;
sentences.i: And Hippolochus begot me, and I say that I was born of him;
sentences.n: Ἱππόλοχος … μ’ is ‘Hippolochus … me’. ἔτικτε is the imperfect of τίκτω, used of a father, ‘begot’ (the house word). φημι γενέσθαι is ‘I say that I was born’: the same fact twice, first as the plain statement and then as his own claim to it.

sentences.t:
πέμπε δέ μ’ ἐς Τροίην, καί μοι μάλα πόλλ’ ἐπέτελλεν
αἰὲν ἀριστεύειν καὶ ὑπείροχον ἔμμεναι ἄλλων,
μηδὲ γένος πατέρων αἰσχυνέμεν, οἳ μέγ’ ἄριστοι
ἔν τ’ Ἐφύρῃ ἐγένοντο καὶ ἐν Λυκίῃ εὐρείῃ.
sentences.tr:
pempe de m’ es Troiēn, kai moi mala poll’ epetellen
aien aristeuein kai hypeirochon emmenai allōn,
mēde genos paterōn aischynemen, hoi meg’ aristoi
en t’ Ephyrēi egenonto kai en Lykiēi eureiēi.
sentences.l:
And he sent me to Troy, and to me very many commands gave,
always to be the best and to be one standing above others,
and not to shame the race of fathers, who by far the best
in Ephyre became and in wide Lycia.
sentences.i: He sent me to Troy and charged me strictly: always to be the best and to stand above the others, and not to shame the line of my fathers, who proved by far the best in Ephyre and in wide Lycia.
sentences.n: πέμπε is the imperfect ‘sent’, and ἐπέτελλεν ‘laid commands on’ takes three infinitives: ἀριστεύειν ‘to be the best’ (from ἄριστος), ὑπείροχον ἔμμεναι ‘to be one who stands above’ (ὑπείροχος is built like ὑπείρεχεν ‘rose above’, 3.210; ἔμμεναι is the epic εἶναι), and μηδὲ … αἰσχυνέμεν ‘and not to shame’ (the epic infinitive of αἰσχύνω). γένος πατέρων is ‘the race of fathers’. οἳ μέγ’ ἄριστοι … ἐγένοντο is ‘who proved by far the best’. The two places, Ephyre (152) and Lycia, are the two sides of Glaucus’ descent, and he is to live up to both.

sentences.t: ταύτης τοι γενεῆς τε καὶ αἵματος εὔχομαι εἶναι.
sentences.tr: tautēs toi geneēs te kai haimatos euchomai einai.
sentences.l: Of this lineage, I tell you, and of this blood I claim to be.”
sentences.i: I tell you, I claim to be of this lineage and this blood.”
sentences.n: τοι is ‘I tell you’, the pronoun worn down to a particle. ταύτης γενεῆς τε καὶ αἵματος is a genitive of origin after εἶναι. γενεή is ‘lineage’ once more, as in 145. εὔχομαι εἶναι is ‘I claim to be’, εὔχομαι with an infinitive: not ‘pray’. The speech ends here, where it began, with his birth.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, γήθησεν δὲ βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: hōs phato, gēthēsen de boēn agathos Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and rejoiced, good at the war-cry, Diomedes;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Diomedes, good at the war-cry, rejoiced;
sentences.n: The paragraph break begins the answer. ὣς φάτο is ‘so he spoke’, closing Glaucus’ speech. γήθησεν is the aorist of γηθέω ‘rejoice’: what he feels is gladness, as the next lines show. βοὴν ἀγαθός is the stock epithet.

sentences.t:
ἔγχος μὲν κατέπηξεν ἐπὶ χθονὶ πουλυβοτείρῃ,
αὐτὰρ ὃ μειλιχίοισι προσηύδα ποιμένα λαῶν·
sentences.tr:
enchos men katepēxen epi chthoni poulyboteirēi,
autar ho meilichioisi prosēuda poimena laōn·
sentences.l:
his spear indeed he fixed in the much-nourishing earth,
but then with gentle ones he addressed the shepherd of the people:
sentences.i: He fixed his spear in the earth that feeds so many, and spoke to the shepherd of the people with gentle words:
sentences.n: ἔγχος μὲν κατέπηξεν ‘he fixed his spear’ is a gesture: he puts the fight aside. The μέν is answered by αὐτὰρ ὅ ‘but then he’. κατέπηξεν is the aorist of καταπήγνυμι, and πουλυβοτείρῃ ‘much-nourishing’ is the stock epithet of the earth. μειλιχίοισι ‘with gentle (words)’ leaves the noun out. ποιμένα λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is Glaucus, and it is the epithet of leaders.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥά νύ μοι ξεῖνος πατρώϊός ἐσσι παλαιός·
sentences.tr: ē rha ny moi xeinos patrōïos essi palaios·
sentences.l: “Truly then, now, to me a guest-friend from my father’s time you are, an old one;
sentences.i: “So then you are a guest-friend of mine from my father’s time, an old one;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥά νύ is ‘truly, then, now’, the cluster for a discovery. ξεῖνος here is the guest-friend, the man tied to a host by hospitality given and returned (the house word), πατρώϊος is ‘from my father’s time’ (inherited), and παλαιός ‘old’ means of long standing. ἐσσι is the epic 2nd singular of εἰμί. The bond descends from fathers to sons.

sentences.t:
Οἰνεὺς γάρ ποτε δῖος ἀμύμονα Βελλεροφόντην
ξείνισ’ ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἐείκοσιν ἤματ’ ἐρύξας·
sentences.tr:
Oineus gar pote dios amymona Bellerophontēn
xeinis’ eni megaroisin eeikosin ēmat’ eryxas·
sentences.l:
For Oeneus once, heavenly, blameless Bellerophon
entertained in his halls, twenty days having kept him;
sentences.i: For heavenly Oeneus once entertained blameless Bellerophon in his halls, keeping him there twenty days;
sentences.n: Οἰνεύς is Oeneus, Tydeus’ father and so Diomedes’ grandfather (5.813). δῖος ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet. ξείνισ’ is ξείνισε ‘entertained as a guest’, and μεγάροισιν is ‘halls’, a plural for one house. ἐείκοσιν is ‘twenty’. ἐρύξας ‘having kept him’ is the verb of 192: a host holds his guest. The Lycian king kept Bellerophon nine days (174), Oeneus twenty.

sentences.t: οἳ δὲ καὶ ἀλλήλοισι πόρον ξεινήϊα καλά·
sentences.tr: hoi de kai allēloisi poron xeinēïa kala·
sentences.l: and they also to one another gave fine guest-gifts;
sentences.i: and the two of them gave each other fine guest-gifts;
sentences.n: οἳ δὲ ‘and they’ is Oeneus and Bellerophon. πόρον is the unaugmented aorist of πορεῖν ‘give’, and ξεινήϊα are the guest-gifts, tokens of the bond that each side keeps. The next unit names them.

sentences.t:
Οἰνεὺς μὲν ζωστῆρα δίδου φοίνικι φαεινόν,
Βελλεροφόντης δὲ χρύσεον δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον
καί μιν ἐγὼ κατέλειπον ἰὼν ἐν δώμασ’ ἐμοῖσι.
sentences.tr:
Oineus men zōstēra didou phoiniki phaeinon,
Bellerophontēs de chryseon depas amphikypellon
kai min egō kateleipon iōn en dōmas’ emoisi.
sentences.l:
Oeneus a belt was giving, shining with crimson,
and Bellerophon a golden double cup,
and it I left behind, going, in my house.
sentences.i: Oeneus gave a belt shining with crimson, and Bellerophon a golden double cup, and I left it behind in my house when I set out.
sentences.n: δίδου is an imperfect of giving, English ‘gave’. ζωστήρ is a belt, and φοίνικι φαεινόν ‘shining with crimson’ has φοῖνιξ, the crimson dye, in the dative of means. δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον is the house ‘double cup’ (the shape is not certain); the second half leaves out the verb, and the English supplies ‘gave’. In καί μιν ἐγὼ κατέλειπον, μιν is the cup (Homer lets μιν stand for a neuter), ‘I left it behind’, and ἰών is ‘going, when I set out’ for Troy. The cup, kept in Diomedes’ house, is the visible sign of the old bond. Our text has no stop between lines 220 and 221, and the two clauses run on, joined by καί.

sentences.t:
Τυδέα δ’ οὐ μέμνημαι, ἐπεί μ’ ἔτι τυτθὸν ἐόντα
κάλλιφ’, ὅτ’ ἐν Θήβῃσιν ἀπώλετο λαὸς Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
Tydea d’ ou memnēmai, epei m’ eti tytthon eonta
kalliph’, hot’ en Thēbēisin apōleto laos Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
But Tydeus I do not remember, since me still small, being,
he left, when in Thebes perished the people of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: But I do not remember Tydeus, since he left me when I was still small, when the army of the Achaeans perished at Thebes.
sentences.n: Τυδέα is the object of μέμνημαι (the perfect of μιμνήσκομαι with a present sense, ‘I remember’). κάλλιφ’ is κατέλιπε ‘he left’, shortened, with the π turned to φ before the rough breathing of the next word. τυτθόν is ‘small’, in the accusative with μ’. Θήβῃσιν is ‘at Thebes’, a plural name, and λαὸς Ἀχαιῶν is ‘the people, the army, of the Achaeans’. The attack on Thebes in which Tydeus died is the one Agamemnon introduces at 4.376–398 (Tydeus’ embassy before it) and Sthenelus recalls at 4.403–410.

sentences.t:
τὼ νῦν σοὶ μὲν ἐγὼ ξεῖνος φίλος Ἄργεϊ μέσσῳ
εἰμί, σὺ δ’ ἐν Λυκίῃ ὅτε κεν τῶν δῆμον ἵκωμαι.
sentences.tr:
tō nyn soi men egō xeinos philos Argeï messōi
eimi, sy d’ en Lykiēi hote ken tōn dēmon hikōmai.
sentences.l:
Therefore now to you I a dear guest-friend in the midst of Argos
am, and you in Lycia, whenever of those people the land I may come to.
sentences.i: So now I am a dear guest-friend to you in the middle of Argos, and you to me in Lycia, whenever I come to the land of those people.
sentences.n: τώ is τῷ ‘therefore’. ἐγὼ ξεῖνος φίλος … εἰμί is ‘I am a dear guest-friend’, with Ἄργεϊ μέσσῳ ‘in the middle of Argos’ (Argos is the land; μέσσος is μέσος). The verb is left out of the second half, σὺ δ’ ἐν Λυκίῃ, ‘and you (are one) in Lycia’. ὅτε κεν … ἵκωμαι is ‘whenever I come’, and τῶν δῆμον is ‘the land of those people’, the Lycians (δῆμος is ‘land’). The bond is mutual, each to host the other in his own country.

sentences.t: ἔγχεα δ’ ἀλλήλων ἀλεώμεθα καὶ δι’ ὁμίλου·
sentences.tr: enchea d’ allēlōn aleōmetha kai di’ homilou·
sentences.l: And the spears of one another let us avoid, even through the throng;
sentences.i: Let us avoid each other’s spears, even as we pass through the throng;
sentences.n: ἔγχεα ἀλλήλων is ‘one another’s spears’. ἀλεώμεθα is the aorist subjunctive of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid, keep clear of’, used as a ‘let us’, with the accusative of what is avoided. καὶ δι’ ὁμίλου is ‘even through the throng’ (ὅμιλος ‘throng’), where avoiding is hardest.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ μὲν γὰρ ἐμοὶ Τρῶες κλειτοί τ’ ἐπίκουροι
κτείνειν ὅν κε θεός γε πόρῃ καὶ ποσσὶ κιχείω,
πολλοὶ δ’ αὖ σοὶ Ἀχαιοὶ ἐναιρέμεν ὅν κε δύνηαι.
sentences.tr:
polloi men gar emoi Trōes kleitoi t’ epikouroi
kteinein hon ke theos ge porēi kai possi kicheiō,
polloi d’ au soi Achaioi enairemen hon ke dynēai.
sentences.l:
For many to me are the Trojans and the famous allies
to kill, whomever a god may grant and with my feet I may reach,
and many in turn to you are the Achaeans to slay, whomever you can.
sentences.i: For there are many Trojans and famous allies for me to kill, whomever a god may grant me and I can reach on foot, and many Achaeans for you in turn to slay, whomever you can.
sentences.n: πολλοὶ μὲν … ἐμοί ‘many for me’ and πολλοὶ δ’ αὖ σοί ‘many in turn for you’ leave out ‘are’. κλειτοί (the same as κλυτοί) ‘famous’ goes with ἐπίκουροι ‘allies’. κτείνειν ‘to kill’ and ἐναιρέμεν ‘to slay’ (the epic infinitive of ἐναίρω) are infinitives saying what the many are for. ὅν κε θεός γε πόρῃ is ‘whomever a god may give (me)’, with πόρῃ the aorist subjunctive of πορεῖν, and καὶ ποσσὶ κιχείω is ‘and I can reach with my feet’ (κιχείω, aorist subjunctive of κιχάνω; ποσσί the epic dative plural of πούς). The γάρ gives his reason: each has enough other enemies.

sentences.t:
τεύχεα δ’ ἀλλήλοις ἐπαμείψομεν, ὄφρα καὶ οἵδε
γνῶσιν ὅτι ξεῖνοι πατρώϊοι εὐχόμεθ’ εἶναι.
sentences.tr:
teuchea d’ allēlois epameipsomen, ophra kai hoide
gnōsin hoti xeinoi patrōïoi euchometh’ einai.
sentences.l:
And armour with one another let us exchange, so that these too
may know that guest-friends from our fathers’ time we claim to be.”
sentences.i: And let us exchange armour with one another, so that these men too may know that we claim to be guest-friends from our fathers’ time.”
sentences.n: ἐπαμείψομεν is an aorist subjunctive with a short vowel, used as ‘let us exchange’, and τεύχεα is ‘armour’. ὄφρα καὶ οἵδε γνῶσιν is ‘so that these too may know’, οἵδε being the men around them in both armies, and γνῶσιν the aorist subjunctive of γιγνώσκω. ξεῖνοι πατρώϊοι is ‘guest-friends from our fathers’ time’, as in 215, and εὐχόμεθ’ εἶναι ‘we claim to be’. The exchange is to show the bond to the men around them. The speech ends here.
